en: Recorded by the disciple Guanding of the teachings of the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty:
Regarding those who resolve their minds through contemplating the marks and signs of the Buddha— if one sees the Tathāgata’s physical body born of parents...
The physical marks are brilliantly manifest;
their clarity and attainment are radiant and dazzling,
such that even Viśvakarman could not have produced them.
The marks and signs of the supreme Wheel-Turning King envelop him; he is rare in the world.
In the heavens above and the earth below, none is like the Buddha;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is likewise no equal.
"May I attain Buddhahood as an Equal Sage and Dharma King.
May I deliver countless and immeasurable sentient beings.
This is the arousal of the bodhicitta through beholding the marks and signs of a Response-Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*), seeking the supreme above and transforming those below.
If one sees the Tathāgata, one knows that the Tathāgata is no Tathāgata;
if one sees the marks and signs, one knows that the marks and signs are not marks and signs.
Both the Tathāgata and the marks are like empty space.
In emptiness there is no Buddha, much less the marks and signs of excellence.
To see the Tathāgata as not the Tathāgata is to see the Tathāgata;
to see the marks as non-marks is to see all marks.
"May I attain Buddhahood as an equal to the Holy Dharma King.
May I deliver countless and boundless sentient beings.
This is the arousal of the bodhicitta through seeing the excellence of the marks and signs, seeking what is superior above and transforming those below.
If one beholds the physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body, there is nothing that does not manifest,
like seeing various forms and images in a bright, clear mirror;
regarding each of his primary and secondary marks, neither ordinary beings nor sages can perceive their limits.
Brahmā could not see its summit;
Maudgalyāyana could not fathom its sound.
The Treatise says:
The formless, supreme essence is neither adorned nor unadorned.
May I attain Buddhahood and become equal to the Holy Dharma King.
This is the bodhicitta generated through beholding the marks and signs of the Buddha as a response to his grace, while seeking the Way above and transforming those below.
If one sees the Tathāgata,
one knows that the Tathāgata’s wisdom profoundly penetrates the characteristics of both transgression and merit, universally illuminating the ten directions;
it is the subtle, wondrous, and pure Dharma-body.
The thirty-two marks are each and every one the mark of reality (lakṣaṇa).
The dharma-realm of the mark of reality is fully complete and without deficiency.
"May I, upon attaining Buddhahood, be equal to the Holy Dharma King.
This constitutes seeing the Buddha through the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
Thus, one generates the bodhicitta by seeking the higher [enlightenment] and transforming those below, and so forth.
How does one generate the bodhicitta by seeing the various miraculous transformations of the Buddha?
If one sees the Tathāgata relying upon fundamental dhyāna.
When one concentrates the mind on a single point, many cannot be attained.
If one ray of light is emitted, it rises from the Avīci Hell up to the Peak of Existence;
the brilliance of the fire blazes forth, making heaven and earth transparently luminous.
"The sun and moon withdraw their layered radiance, and the light of heaven is hidden and does not appear.
May I, upon attaining Buddhahood, equal the Sage Dharma-King... and so forth.
If one perceives the Tathāgata, one should do so according to the principle of the non-arising nature of the Tathāgata.
Without employing dualistic conceptions toward sentient beings,
he is able to cause each and every being to see the Buddha as if he were standing alone before them.
"May I, upon attaining Buddhahood, be equal to the Holy Dharma King," and so forth.
If one sees the Tathāgata,
he abides in the samādhi of the Tathāgatagarbha and manifests the four modes of deportment throughout the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions.
Yet they have never wavered from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
May I attain Buddhahood equal to the Holy Dharma King, and so forth.
If one sees the Tathāgata...
It is non-dual and indistinguishable from all supernatural transformations (ṛddhi-prātihārya).
The Tathāgata performs supernatural transformations, and supernatural transformations manifest as the Tathāgata; it is an unconditioned (avyākṛta) transformation of a transformation.
Transformations produce further transformations,
which are inexhaustible;
all are inconceivable.
All these perform the Buddha-work through the true nature (*dharmatā*).
May I, upon attaining Buddhahood, be equal to the Holy Dharma King, and so forth.
How does one hear various teachings and give rise to the bodhicitta?
Whether from the Buddha or from spiritual friends,
or from a scripture, one hears a single phrase concerning arising and ceasing.
One immediately understands that worldly and world-transcending phenomena arise and perish anew, shifting from moment to moment;
it is only through precepts, wisdom, liberation, and tranquility that one attains the truth.
"May I, upon attaining Buddhahood, be able to expound the pure path," and so forth.
Or, upon hearing of arising and ceasing,
one immediately understands that the Four Noble Truths are all neither arising nor ceasing.
In the void there are no thorns; how can they be extracted?
Who suffers? Who accumulates [suffering]? Who practices? Who realizes?
Ultimately pure, both subject and object are quiescent.
"May I, upon attaining Buddhahood, be able to expound the pure path," and so forth.
Or, upon hearing of arising and ceasing,
one immediately understands that arising and ceasing are dualistic in contrast to non-arising and non-ceasing.
Neither arising and ceasing nor non-arising and non-ceasing is the Middle;
this Middle Way is pure and uniquely transcendent,
emerging beyond both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
"May I, upon attaining Buddhahood, be able to expound the supreme path for the sake of sentient beings,
so that they may emerge alone and unattached, like a lotus rising from the water or the moon dwelling in the sky," and so forth;
or one may hear [the teaching on] arising and ceasing.
One immediately understands arising-and-ceasing, non-arising-and-non-ceasing, that which is neither arising-and-ceasing nor non-arising-and-non-ceasing.
One simultaneously illuminates both arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing; it is three in one and one in three.
The Dharma-realm is secret and eternally endowed with bliss.
May I attain Buddhahood so that I may expound the secret treasury for the sake of sentient beings.
It is as when a person of merit takes a stone and turns it into a jewel, or takes poison and turns it into medicine, and so forth.
If one hears of "non-arising," it refers to the fact that while the followers of the Two Vehicles have no further birth within the three realms, Bodhisattvas have not yet attained non-arising.
If one hears of "non-arising," [it is in this sense].
This means that for all three vehicles, there is no birth within the triple world.
If one hears of non-arising,
it is not the domain of the two vehicles, but belongs only to the bodhisattvas.
A bodhisattva first has no birth by way of physical fragmentation,
and subsequently no birth by way of transformation.
If they hear of "non-arising"— the non-arising of one thing, the non-arising of all things— [they realize this].
If one hears of the immeasurable, a single phrase is exemplified in this way.
"Hearing of the immeasurable" refers to the four truths and sixteen aspects of the two vehicles' path of skillful means, and so forth.
They consider it to be immeasurable.
If they hear of the immeasurable,
those of the Two Vehicles, being preoccupied with their own subduing of afflictions, are unable to transform others.
By means of these immeasurables, the bodhisattva removes their own delusions and transforms others.
If one hears of these immeasurables,
one might think they are not shared by the two vehicles but belong only to bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattva, by means of this, severs the dust and sands within the realm and also subdues the dust and sands outside the realm; if one hears of them as being immeasurable,
[one likewise attains mastery].
This means that while the two vehicles do not possess this [wisdom], it belongs exclusively to the bodhisattvas.
Bodhisattvas employ it to sever the dust-like afflictions within and without the realms,
and they also subdue ignorance.
If one hears that "immeasurability" applies only to bodhisattvas,
and that bodhisattvas employ it to subdue and sever ignorance,
then if one hears the single phrase "non-action," the principle is likewise the same.
If one hears of "non-action" (anabhisamskāra),
it means that it is not something created by Buddhas, devas, humans, or asuras.
The followers of the two vehicles realize this non-action.
The *Suvikrāntavikrāmi-paripṛcchā* states:
"We have studied non-action and have already attained realization;
yet the bodhisattvas are unable to attain it," and so forth.
If one hears of non-action (anabhisaṃskāra),
it is said that all three vehicles are able to realize it.
If one hears of non-action...
This means it is not the realm of the two vehicles, let alone that of ordinary beings.
A bodhisattva shatters provisional non-action to realize true non-action.
If one hears of this non-action, [one realizes it].
This means that the provisional non-action realizes the ultimate non-action.
If one grasps this intent,
then upon hearing a single phrase, one will penetrate all phrases.
"Up to the point where there is no obstruction regarding all phrases and all dharmas," and so forth.
Now, the meaning of "a single teaching being understood in various ways" is difficult to clarify;
therefore, it shall be explained again by means of a verse from the *Śāstra*.
If one says, "Those phenomena produced by causes and conditions—
I declare them to be empty," then since they are produced by causes and conditions, how could they be empty?
One must analyze the causes and conditions until they are exhausted before one can realize emptiness.
To call "emptiness" itself "emptiness" is also termed "provisional designation.
This is because conditioned phenomena are weak and fragile, lacking independent existence.
It is established through the convergence of various conditions; because it relies upon conditions, this "provisionality" (jia) is not the provisionality of expedient means (shiquan).
It is also termed the meaning of the Middle Way.
To be free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism is called the Middle Way, not the Middle Way that is Buddha-nature.
If one interprets it in this way,
although all three propositions are empty, [it remains so].
If [the conventional] cannot even be established as identical to emptiness,
how much less can it be identical to the provisional or identical to the middle?
This is the meaning of the Four Noble Truths in terms of arising and ceasing.
If dharmas produced by causes and conditions do not require destruction, their essence is emptiness itself;
yet they cannot be immediately identified as the provisional or the middle. Even if they are provisionally designated as the provisional or the middle, these all conform to and enter into emptiness.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are themselves empty, lacking a master or a self;
and because even the conventional is itself empty, being merely a provisional designation.
The middle is also emptiness itself, for it is free from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
Although these three formulations differ in expression, they all accord with the entry into emptiness;
this does not involve the analytical negation of phenomena characteristic of the Two Vehicles.
Advancement is neither distinct nor complete;
it is merely the meaning of the three animals crossing the river together through the void.
If one were to say that this is precisely emptiness, precisely the provisional, and precisely the middle, [it would be a misunderstanding].
The three types proceed in succession, each being distinct.
As for the statement that the three terms are all empty:
they are empty because they lack a master.
It is empty because it is established as a mere fiction; it is empty because it is boundless.
These three aspects are all provisional designations.
They are provisional because they equally possess names.
As for "all three terms are 'middle'":
they are all "middle" because they are the middle truth, the middle capacity, and the middle reality.
Regarding the statement, "This attains the particular while losing the perfect," and so forth:
if one says that emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are identical—
such that though they are three, they are one, and though they are one, they are three.
They do not obstruct one another.
Regarding the statement that "the three kinds are all empty," it means that they are severed from both speech and thought.
That all three are conventional means that they exist merely as names;
that all three are intermediate means...
Because it is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*),
it is designated simply by the name "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*);
it thus fully possesses the provisional and the middle.
Wu-k'ung immediately realized the falsity within the provisional;
it is the same for the rest.
One should know that by hearing a single dharma, [one realizes all].
To give rise to various understandings and establish various vows is precisely to generate various forms of the bodhicitta;
this can also be understood in this way.
In that Pure Land, when the Dharma practiced by the assembly of followers declines,
they undergo suffering and give rise to transgressions;
their subsequent arousal of the bodhicitta is to be understood according to the previous examples.
I shall not record them in further detail.
Since what has been explained above is already extensive,
I shall now conclude by summarizing it through the three types of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
However, since the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not even a single dharma,
how can one investigate it by means of three or four?
It is for this reason that we now speak of one, two, three, and four.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is that which is deluded; suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) are that which causes delusion.

Regarding the degrees of intensity of the deluding [subject] and the relationship between the deluded [object]—whether immediate or remote—there are four types of suffering and its origin when distinguished according to the internal and external realms.
According to the capacities of the faculties, there are differences of one, two, three, or four ways of grasping the principle, and so forth.
Within the realm, for those of dull capacity who are deluded regarding the Truth, suffering and its origin are heavy;
for those of sharp capacity who are deluded regarding the Truth, suffering and its origin are light.
The same applies to those outside the realm regarding their sharpness or dullness and the lightness or heaviness [of their afflictions].
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is that which is to be understood;
the Path and Cessation are that which enables understanding.
Regarding what is understood, there is the presence or absence of a subject that understands, and the understanding itself may be skillful or clumsy.
Within the realm [of ordinary beings], the understanding of those with dull faculties is clumsy because it lacks a subject that understands;
the understanding of those with sharp faculties is skillful because their subject that understands is also present.
The distinction between those of sharp and dull faculties outside the realm, as well as the presence or absence of skill and clumsiness, is likewise so. Why is this?
Because since phenomena and principle are already distinct, the resulting delusions and confusions are also extreme.
For example, if both father and son are struck by a stranger, the anger felt toward him is equally intense for both;
here, anger illustrates *saṃudaya* (the origin of suffering), while being struck illustrates *duḥkha* (suffering).
If one asserts that afflictions (*kleśa*) are identical to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), this signifies the mutual identity of principle and phenomenon.
If suffering arises, it is light.
In reality, it is not as if bone and flesh were two separate things; when father and son scold or strike one another, the pain is slight.
The same applies to coarse and fine, branch and root, common and specific, pervasive and non-pervasive, difficult and easy, and so forth.
Some say that within the realm, suffering and its accumulation are heavy because they involve stagnation;
outside the realm, emergence and transcendence are light.
Alternatively, it is shallow because the afflictions are within the realm (*dhātu*),
and deep because the afflictions are outside the realm.
Or it is said:
Within the boundary, it is considered clumsy because one conforms to the intentions of others;
outside the boundary, it is considered skillful because one follows one's own intentions.
Or it is said:
It is skillful because it accords with the capacities [of beings] within the realm;
it is clumsy because it does not accord with the capacities outside the realm.
Or, it is said:
Because there is subject and object within the realm, it is coarse;
because there is no subject and object outside the realm, it is subtle.
Or it is said:
The minor paths within the realm are considered subtle because they culminate at the City of Transformation;
the major roads outside the realm are considered coarse because they culminate at the Place of Jewels.
Or it is said:
Because adventitious defilements exist within the realm, they are considered branches;
because they share the same essence as that which is outside the realm, they are considered the root. Or it is said:
Because they exist within the realm (*dhātu*), those of the internal [realm] are the root;
because they exist outside the realm, those of the external [realm] are the branches.
Or it is said:
It is "common" because it is shared by both small and large [beings] within the realm;
it is "distinct" because it exists solely among the great ones outside the realm.
Or, as some say:
Because it is partial within the boundary, it is small; because it is shallow, it is distinct.
Because it is circular outside the boundary, it is great; because there is no separation, it is pervasive.
Or it is said:
It is not all-pervasive because it is limited within the realm;
it is all-pervasive because its circumference extends beyond the realm to the extent of the dharma-realm.
Or, it is said:
Within the realm, it is "pervasive" because it is shared by all noble ones (ārya);
outside the realm, it is "non-pervasive" because it exists solely as a great object of focus for the solitary [Buddha].
Alternatively, it is said:
Because they employ the skillful means of the two vehicles within the realm [of the three realms], they are difficult to sever;
because they rely solely on unimpeded wisdom beyond the realm, they are easy to sever.
Such various explanations are given in mutual relation.
If one were to apply these now, they would be easy to resolve.
To distinguish between shallow and deep, or light and heavy,
is the method for observing the mind through gradual stages.
If one treats the four truths as a single reality without making distinctions,

this is the intent of the "perfect contemplation" (yuan guan). If one treats them as having varying degrees of lightness and gravity relative to one another, [this is the intent of the "gradual contemplation"].
This refers to the mind of indeterminate contemplation.
Since these are all the doctrinal characteristics (dharmalakṣaṇa) of the Mahāyāna, they must be understood.
If one perceives this meaning, [one will not fall into error].
One immediately knows these three types:
those manifested gradually and those manifested indeterminately.
"The Perfect and Sudden [Teaching] reveals this," and so forth.
Question: Since there are four types of compendia (*saṃgraha*), [how is this so?]
What are the two aspects of the fruit of suffering? Answer:
When afflictions follow along with liberation, there are four types of accumulation.
When liberation follows from delusion, it merely results in two types of death;
for example, in the Lesser Vehicle, when liberation follows from delusion, there are both the death of seeing the truths (*darśana-mārga*) and the death of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
If liberation follows from delusion, it is simply the death of fragmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*).
Question:
Suffering and its origin may indeed be phenomena produced by causes and conditions;
why is this the case for the Path and Cessation?
Answer: Suffering and its origin are that which is to be destroyed;
the path and cessation are that which destroys.
Both the destroyer and the destroyed are designated by their names because they are both dharmas produced by causes and conditions.
Thus, the Great Sūtra says:
"By the cessation of ignorance, one obtains the blazing lamp of *samyak-saṃbodhi*."
This, too, is a causal condition.
Question:
The dharma-nature is that which is deluded about.
Why are there two? Why are there four?
Answer: Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) conforms to both the provisional and the ultimate, there are two.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) follows the faculties and conditions; therefore, there are four.
If one perceives this meaning, one will likewise perceive the characteristics of seeing, hearing, and so forth, up to the arising of transgressions.
For example, the fourfold analysis is explained at length, and so forth.
Regarding the point that this [nature] is revealed through the great vows:
the meaning has already been clarified by the preceding investigation of the dharma-nature and the hearing of the Dharma.
For those who have not yet fully understood, [the text] further explains this in terms of the Four Great Vows.
Furthermore, within the Four Noble Truths, the upward seeking and downward transforming are mostly clarified through understanding;
within the Four Great Vows, the upward seeking and downward transforming are mostly clarified through aspiration.
Furthermore, within the Four Noble Truths, the aspiration for supreme enlightenment and the transformation of others are generally explained in relation to the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
within the Four Great Vows, these are mostly explained in relation to the Buddhas of the future.
Moreover, within the Four Noble Truths, the aspiration for supreme enlightenment and the transformation of others are mostly explained in relation to the various faculties [of sentient beings].
Within the Four Great Vows, the upward seeking and downward transforming are specifically explained in relation to the faculty of mind (*manas*).
This distinction is made for the sake of easy understanding;
those who grasp the underlying meaning need not rely on it.
Now, the mind does not arise in isolation; it must depend upon the arising of conditions.
The faculty of the mind (*manas*) is the cause, and mental objects (*dharmas*) are the condition; that which arises from them is the produced phenomenon.
These faculties and objects—the agent, the object, and the three characteristics—constantly shift and change.
I secretly rise and secretly prostrate.
Arising and ceasing in every new moment, they do not abide for even an instant;
they flash and flicker like a bolt of lightning.
Swift and rapid as a rushing torrent:
form is like a bubble, sensation like foam, perception like a mirage, volitional formations like a city of Gandharvas, and consciousness like a magical illusion.
All that is relied upon—the land, fields, houses, wife, children, and property—is likewise so.
In a single thought one may perish, vanishing in an instant;
the three realms are impermanent, a single casket of pervasive suffering.
When the four mountains close in, there is no place to flee or hide.
One should simply concentrate one's mind upon precept, concentration, and wisdom;
vertically shattering inverted views and horizontally cutting across the sea of death, one transcends the flow of existence.
As the Sūtra says:
In the past, because I and you did not see the Four Noble Truths,
we have long wandered in saṃsāra.
Since the burning house is like this, how can you remain immersed in it, indulging in negligence and sporting in play?
Therefore, out of compassion, one gives rise to the Four Great Vows to uproot suffering and bestow happiness.
This is like Śākyamuni’s vision of the plowing fields,
and resembles Maitreya’s contemplation of the ruined terraces.
This is precisely its meaning.
Because one clearly realizes the Four Noble Truths, it is not the ninefold bondage;
because one gives rise to the Four Great Vows, it is not the single liberation.
This is the true and correct arousal of the bodhicitta that is neither bound nor liberated;
this meaning is now clearly elucidated.
Next, one simply observes the arising of a single thought-moment when the sense faculties and their objects encounter one another.
That which gives rise and that which is given rise to are both none other than emptiness.
It is falsely claimed that the mind arises;
yet this arising has neither intrinsic nature nor extrinsic nature.
It possesses neither a common nature nor a causeless nature;
when it arises, it does not come from self, other, both, or from nowhere;
when it passes away, it does not go toward the east, west, south, or north.
This mind does not exist within, without, or in between the two;
nor does it exist eternally of itself.
It exists only as a name, which is called "mind."
This word neither abides nor does it not abide, because it is ungraspable;
thus, arising is itself non-arising, and there is also no non-arising.
Both existence and non-existence are quiescent.
Ordinary fools claim that the wise know non-existence;
like the moon in water, they experience joy upon its acquisition and sorrow upon its loss.
Yet the Great Man is entirely free from both acceptance and rejection, experiencing neither elation nor distress.
Reflections, images, and magical illusions are also like this.
The *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā* states:
"Suffering is non-arising; origination is non-assembly; the path is non-dual; cessation is non-birth."
The Great Sūtra says:
"Understanding that suffering is without suffering, there is true reality;
and so on, up to understanding that cessation is without cessation, there is true reality."
Since the aggregates are themselves emptiness,
one should not pursue them like a thirsty deer chasing a mirage.
Since suffering is itself emptiness...
One should not be like that foolish monkey who grasps at the moon in the water.
Since the Way is itself emptiness,
one should not say, "I practice emptiness," or "I do not practice emptiness," or "I do not practice non-emptiness."
Regarding the parable of the raft:
even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone that which is not the Dharma.
Since cessation is itself emptiness.
One should not say that regarding the life-span of sentient beings, someone perishes here and realizes extinction there.
Since birth and death are themselves empty, how could they be abandoned?
Since nirvana is itself empty, how could it be attained?
The Sūtra says:
"I do not wish for there to be the cultivation of the path within dharmas that are unarisen,
whether it be the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path."
I do not wish for there to be the attainment of fruits within the state of non-arising dharmas.
By this same principle, it should also be said regarding those from the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to the arhat.
I do not wish for form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness to exist within the dharma of non-arising.
I do not wish for desire, hatred, or delusion to exist within the dharma of non-arising.
However, out of compassion for sentient beings, one gives rise to vows to uproot the two kinds of suffering and bestow the two kinds of happiness.
Because one has realized that suffering and its origin are empty, there are no nine bonds;
because one has realized that the path and cessation are empty, there is no single liberation.
This is what is meant by the true and correct arousal of the bodhicitta that is neither bound nor liberated.
This meaning is clearly revealed by observing the arising of a single thought-moment within the faculties and their objects.
The arising of the mind is provisional;
this provisionally named mind serves as the basis for both delusion and awakening.
This means that the Four Noble Truths possess immeasurable aspects.
In the three realms there are no separate dharmas; they are created solely by the one mind.
The mind is like a skilled painter who creates all manner of colors;
the mind constructs the six destinies.
One discriminates and examines immeasurable varieties,
namely: such views and cravings are the characteristics of the accumulation of light and heavy [karma] within the realm,
and the characteristics of the accumulation of light and heavy [karma] outside the realm.

Such is the nature of birth and death as the light and heavy aspects of suffering within the realms of segmentation; it is likewise the nature of the light and heavy aspects of suffering beyond the realms.
By turning this mind back upon itself, one gives rise to liberation.
It is like a painter who washes away all colors and applies fresh pigments—
namely, contemplating the impurity of the body up to contemplating the impermanence of the mind.
In this way, the factors of the path lead through the transformation city.
One contemplates the body as empty of the body, and so on, up to contemplating the mind as empty of the mind.
Within emptiness, there is no impermanence,
and so on, up to no impurity.
In this way, the factors of the path lead directly to the transformation city.
One contemplates the body as impermanent;
impermanence is itself emptiness, and so on until one contemplates the dharma-nature of the body.
It is neither eternal nor impermanent, neither empty nor non-empty.
This applies even to the contemplation of the mind.
In this way, the factors of the path wind through to the place of the treasure.
Contemplate the dharma-nature of the body as being neither pure nor impure, while simultaneously illuminating both purity and impurity; and so on,
up to contemplating the dharma-nature of the mind.
Constantly and simultaneously observing both the permanent and the impermanent—
thus the factors of the path lead directly to the place of treasure.
When such a person perceives the truths and attains cessation, they are named a Srotāpanna.
When this person contemplates cessation, it is called the third fruit.
When this person perceives cessation, it is called the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*).

When this person contemplates cessation, it is called "thinning," "detachment," and "having completed what was to be done," up to "eradicating the latent tendencies," which is called a *pratyekabuddha*.
The extinction of the delusions of views and thought is called the Ten Abodes;
the extinction of the dust-like and sand-like delusions is called the Ten Practices and the Ten Dedications;
and the extinction of ignorance is called the Ten Grounds, Equal Enlightenment, and Sublime Enlightenment.
When this person extinguishes the afflictions of views and thoughts as numerous as motes of dust, it is called the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

When ignorance (*avidyā*) is extinguished, it is called the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*), the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), equal enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), and wondrous enlightenment (*pratyakṣa-bodhi*).
Thus, one distinguishes the differences in the cessation of the path through these sixteen gates.
Furthermore, regarding all the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
though they are incalculably and ineffably manifold when analyzed and reckoned,
one perceives them without error, as clearly as looking at fruit in the palm of one's hand.
All arise from the mind and do not come from any other place.
